title: How to Preach the Psalms
subtitle: A practical guide to preaching the Psalms, handling Hebrew poetry, lament, and praise in the pulpit so the sermon teaches a congregation how to pray.

sections.title: You Are Holding Poetry
sections.body:
The Psalms do not argue. They sing. Preach them like an epistle and you kill them.

Paul builds a case. He reasons, he concludes, he moves from premise to verdict, and your sermon can follow the track he laid. The Psalms do not work that way. They circle. They repeat. They say the same thing twice in different words because Hebrew poetry is built on parallelism, not progression. The second line is not new information. It is the first line felt more deeply. When you flatten a psalm into three propositional points, you have translated music into a memo. The people get the content and lose the thing the content was carried in.

The first discipline of preaching a psalm is to slow down and feel its shape before you outline it. Where does it turn. Where does it repeat. What image carries the weight. The form is not decoration around the message. The form is part of the message.

sections.title: Preach the Image, Do Not Explain It Away
sections.body:
A psalm gives you a green pasture, a hunted deer, bones that melt like wax, a God who is a rock and a shield and a horn. These are not illustrations of the point. They are the point.

The lazy preacher reads the image and immediately translates it into an abstraction. The Lord is my shepherd becomes God provides for our needs, and the sheep are gone, the pasture is gone, the whole world the psalm built has been bulldozed for a doctrine. Do the opposite. Stand inside the image. Make your people smell the grass and hear the still water. Let them feel what it is to be a sheep that does not have to find its own food or fight its own enemies. The doctrine is in there, but it arrives through the senses, the way the psalmist meant it to.

This takes nerve, because describing an image feels less rigorous than explaining a concept. It is not. It is harder, and it is what the text is actually doing.

sections.title: Let Lament Be Lament
sections.body:
Most of the Psalter is complaint. The church has quietly agreed to skip it.

We preach the comfort psalms and the praise psalms and we leave the long, bitter ones alone. How long, O Lord. Why have you forsaken me. My tears have been my food day and night. These are not the prayers of weak faith. They are inspired Scripture, given to us by the Spirit, and a congregation that never hears them learns that grief has no place in church. So when grief comes, and it always comes, your people have no language for it and no permission to use it. They suffer in silence and assume their darkness is a failure of belief.

Preach a lament and do not rush to fix it. Do not tack a happy ending onto a psalm that does not have one. Some laments end in trust, and some end in the dark, and the honest ones teach your people that they can bring God the worst of it without losing him. You are not only teaching them a text. You are teaching them they are allowed to pray when it hurts.

sections.title: The Psalms Were His Prayer Book
sections.body:
Jesus prayed these. From the cross he prayed Psalm 22. This is not a clever application. It is the deepest layer of the text.

The psalmist cries out of a suffering he half understands, and then the true sufferer comes, the one of whom David was only a shadow, and he prays the same words from inside a forsakenness none of us will ever know. My God, my God, why have you forsaken me. When you preach a lament, you are preaching the prayer book of the man of sorrows. When you preach a psalm of the king, you are preaching toward the King the psalm was always reaching for. The praise psalms find their voice in the only one who ever praised the Father perfectly.

This keeps the Psalms from becoming mere emotional weather. They are not just about how we feel. They are about the One who entered our feelings, prayed our prayers, and carried our laments to the place where they were answered.

sections.title: You Are Handing Them a Tongue
sections.body:
The aim of preaching a psalm is not that your people understand the psalm. It is that they pray it.

The Psalter is the church's oldest school of prayer. For three thousand years the people of God have learned how to speak to him by borrowing these words when their own ran out. When you preach a psalm well, you do not send your people home with a lecture about ancient Hebrew worship. You send them home with words in their mouth for the next time they cannot find any. The next sleepless night. The next hospital waiting room. The next morning the praise comes easy and they need somewhere to put it.

Preach so that when the day comes, your people reach for this psalm without thinking. That is the test of preaching the Psalms. Not whether they admired the sermon. Whether, six months later, in the dark, the words come back.
